newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke - Conservatives winning on EU, economy.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke - Conservatives winning on EU, economy.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Thursday the economy and Europe were vote-winners for his Conservative Party, adding that he could yet be one of the politicians voting against membership of a single European currency.
"I think we are beating the Labour Party on Europe, beating the Labour Party on tax, I think we're beating the Labour Party on the economy," Clarke told told BBC radio.
He said an opinion poll in Wednesday' Guardian newspaper, which showed the opposition Labour Party's lead slashed to five points from 14, reflected that.
But three other polls out overnight, put Labour's lead at 19 to 21 points. Elections are due in a week's time.
Clarke said the government's policy of keeping options open over joining a European single currency enjoyed wide support.

"As with the general public, the overwhelming majority of people in British business...say we should keep our option open, we should exercise the maximum influence of the UK whether we join it or not."
But he said no-one should assume he would push for British membership of European economic and monetary union.
"We don't even know yet, whether it is going to start on time," Clarke said, adding that he would never agree to handing over control of tax and spending.

"When it comes to taking the choice, I could be one of those against it," Clarke said. "I'm totally against fudging the criteria for example. But striking out now the option of joining is not in the national interest."

He said Prime Minister John Major had strongly defended that view and said it would remain the government's policy if the Conservatives are re-elected on May 1. "He will form a government on the basis of the manifesto. You can't form a government on any basis except that which you have fought the election," Clarke said.

But he refused to answer questions about large number of Conservative parliamentary candidates who are alleged to have rejected the government's line over EMU. Businessman Paul Sykes, who has contributed to the campaign funds of anti-European candidates has said 231 have accepted his offer.
